cues: Guess what this sugar cube weighs?
It is not sugar.
It is a scrap of a neutron star,
the collapsed core left behind
when a massive star explodes as a supernova.
Now squeeze about 1.4 times the mass of our Sun
into a ball only 20 kilometers across.
Packed that tightly,
a piece the size of a sugar cube
would weigh about a billion tons on Earth.
But if you could carry it home,
it would not stay small.
Without the star's gravity holding it together,
it would burst apart violently.
And deeper inside,
nobody knows for sure what the matter becomes.
Some models suggest
it might even break down into free quarks.
A spoonful of star you can only weigh with math.
What question would you ask it?

A day longer than a year?
On Venus, yes.
One spin on its axis takes about 243 Earth days,
but one trip around the Sun
takes only about 225.
And it spins backward
compared with most planets,
so the Sun would rise in the west.
Here is the twist.
Because it spins backward while it orbits,
sunrise to sunrise is much shorter:
about 117 Earth days.
Why does it spin backward?
Nobody knows for sure.
A giant impact long ago,
or tides from its thick atmosphere,
might have flipped it.
So which is longer on Venus, a day or a year?
It depends on which day you mean.
